title: Who Is Rohan Naidu? The Hyderabad Boy Who Dropped Out of Engineering School — and Just Discovered a New Kind of Cosmic Object
excerpt: At 18, Rohan Naidu left engineering, bought his first plane ticket, and chased the earliest light in the universe. His 'black hole star,' published in Nature this week, is rewriting what astronomers thought they knew about cosmic dawn.
body:
The Discovery That Stopped Astronomers in Their Tracks

On August 12, 2026, when the journal Nature published a paper titled "A gas-enshrouded and gas-reddened black hole at cosmic dawn," the astronomy world took notice. The lead author was Rohan Naidu, a young Indian-born astrophysicist, and the subject was something nobody had confirmed before: a black hole star.

https://x.com/livemint/status/2089254629754445982

The object, called MoM-BH*-1, is a cosmic chimera — part black hole, part star, wrapped in a vast envelope of gas the size of our entire solar system. It formed just 660 million years after the Big Bang, contains a black hole 100,000 times the mass of the Sun, and blazes 100 billion times brighter than an average star. Nothing in existing databases of billions of known objects matches it.

"It is a very special thing to find an object with no comparison. MoM-BH*-1 is one in a billion!"

Naidu and his team stumbled on it while running the Mirage or Miracle (MoM) survey on NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, a project designed to identify the farthest, oldest galaxies in the universe. What they found instead may rewrite the story of how the universe's earliest supermassive black holes — including the one at the center of our own Milky Way — came to exist.

From Hyderabad to the Stars

Rohan Naidu grew up in Hyderabad. Like millions of Indian students, he enrolled in engineering school — and like a vanishingly small number of them, he walked away. At 18, in what his MIT biography describes as "a Bollywood-esque plot twist," he dropped out, bought the first plane ticket of his life, and flew to Singapore to join the inaugural class of 150 students at Yale-NUS College.

It was a gamble that paid off spectacularly. In Singapore, he fell in love with astronomy. He studied blazars — supermassive black holes shooting jets of energy across the cosmos — in the Chilean Andes under Prof. Charles Bailyn. An exchange stint at Yale with Prof. Pascal Oesch sharpened his focus on the early universe. By the time he reached Harvard for his PhD under Prof. Charlie Conroy, Naidu was surveying the Milky Way's outermost reaches, hunting for ancient "immigrant" galaxies that had been swallowed by our own.

His doctoral work on the H3 Survey — mapping the Milky Way's stellar halo using more than 150,000 spectra from the 6.5-meter MMT telescope — produced a comprehensive anatomy of our galaxy's merger history stretching back billions of years.

The James Webb Telescope's First Explorer

After earning his PhD, Naidu moved to MIT's Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research on a NASA Hubble Postdoctoral Fellowship, one of the most competitive awards in observational astronomy. He later became a Pappalardo Fellow at MIT Physics — a position reserved for the department's most promising early-career researchers.

It was at MIT that Naidu became one of the first astronomers to use the James Webb Space Telescope after its launch. In May 2025, he and 45 colleagues announced MoM-z14, the farthest galaxy ever detected — a system that existed just 280 million years after the Big Bang, shattering previous distance records. The discovery was so unexpected that the galaxy was 182 times brighter than models predicted it should be.

"With Webb, we are able to see farther than humans ever have before, and it looks nothing like what we predicted, which is both challenging and exciting."

But it was the Little Red Dots that would consume Naidu's attention. These mysterious, compact, intensely red objects were showing up in virtually every JWST image of the early universe. "They are in every single image the telescope takes," Naidu told Scientific American earlier this year. "We have to find out about them if we want to tell a complete story about the early universe."

Black Hole Stars: A New Chapter in Cosmic History

Traditional models couldn't explain the Little Red Dots. They didn't look like ordinary galaxies. They didn't behave like standard black holes. After three years of what Naidu describes as "relentless community effort," he and his collaborators arrived at a radical hypothesis: these objects were black hole stars — black holes enveloped in dense gas that radiate energy in a manner reminiscent of stellar phenomena, but on a spectacular, solar-system-sized scale.

The August 2026 Nature paper provided the proof. MoM-BH*-1 was so luminous that it outshined its entire host galaxy. Almost all the light astronomers were seeing came directly from the black hole and its gas cocoon, not from any surrounding stars. The redness wasn't caused by cosmic dust, as previously thought, but by the gas itself — a finding that could explain why the earliest supermassive black holes grew far larger than cosmological models allowed.

"We argue that Black Hole Stars may be powering all of JWST's Little Red Dots," Naidu said. "Which is to say, this channel of making massive black holes must be very common, to the point where every massive black hole — like the Milky Way's — may have gone through this phase."

Why It Matters Beyond the Telescope

Speaking to The Guardian, Naidu placed the discovery in a sweeping context. Black hole stars, he said, "may govern when stars are able to form and when they cease forming, setting the course for everything that follows from star formation: the birth of planets, the rise of life, the emergence of species that may one day piece together this entire history."

At just 63 published papers and 1,700 citations, Naidu has already established himself as one of the most productive young astronomers of his generation. Starting in December 2026, he will use more JWST time to probe further into black hole stars, investigating their actual size and atmospheric composition. He has since moved from MIT to the University of Hawai'i, continuing to push the frontier of early-universe astronomy.

The Poet Who Watches Test Cricket

Outside the observatory, Naidu is a quiz-bowl and trivia enthusiast, a published poet, and — in a detail that will resonate with any Indian diaspora reader — "always down to watch test cricket." In a field dominated by meticulous data reduction and statistical rigor, he retains a humanist's eye for storytelling. His survey names read like literary titles: Mirage or Miracle. His descriptions of ancient galaxies — "immigrant galaxies that have been assimilated by our galaxy" — carry an unmistakable echo of the diaspora experience itself.

From dropping out of an engineering program in Hyderabad to discovering an entirely new category of cosmic object with the most powerful telescope ever built, Rohan Naidu's trajectory is a reminder that the Indian diaspora's contributions to human knowledge extend far beyond the boardrooms and startups that tend to dominate headlines. Sometimes they extend to the edge of the observable universe — and 660 million years past the beginning of time.
